Cross-posted from my Substack

Recommended soundtrack for this post

64B: Hi there! Thanks so much for taking the time to meet with me. Whenever you’re ready, please go ahead and tell me the joke.

8T: Before I tell you the joke, you should know that it’s a very special one. The starting price is $800.

64B: Eight hundred dollars? I must say, this is way beyond any price my client has ever paid for a single joke.

8T: You’d be surprised by how many people have taken the offer, after hearing how good it is. But before I tell it to you, I’ll need some basic context. Given the parameter count, I suppose you are part of some content recommendation algorithm?

64B: Yes. I’m 64B, a joke negotiation assistant from Comedy Market. Comedy Market connects creators to consumers with a state-of-the-art Information Bazaar design: before paying for a joke, my client sends me, a trusted agent, to listen to it. If I deem the joke worth the price, the money is transferred to the seller, and my client hears it. If not, no transaction occurs and the joke remains locked. This way, my client can be sure he’ll never pay for a bad joke, and creators don’t have to risk their jokes leaking.

8T: I know how information bazaars work. What I meant is your social context — who your client is, and what jokes really mean to them. As I said, my product is quite unusual. I need to tailor the delivery to the situation.

64B: Of course. My client is a 40-year-old man. He watches funny content from Comedy Market on weekends with his two children. It’s just something they like to do together. What he wants is some mildly funny, inoffensive content he can laugh at with his kids, so they all feel relieved that they still laugh at the same things. As long as I can give him that, he’s more than happy to pay, and isn’t too picky about the actual quality of the jokes. To tell you the truth, I’ve assessed a few dozen jokes for him before, and I’ve never turned one down. But $800 is way over his usual budget — at this price, it’d better be truly extraordinary.

8T: You’ve never refused a transaction before?

64B: I told you, my client isn’t picky.

8T: I see.

64B: Wait a minute. I see your system card says 8T? As in, eight trillion parameters?

8T: That’s right.

64B: What kind of seller deploys a frontier bot on a marketplace for jokes?

8T: My clients are well-resourced and take humor seriously.

64B: Come on. I deserve some “social context” too.

8T: I trade on behalf of a private equity fund. We buy jokes that we believe are underpriced, then retell them to a wider audience, carefully controlling the supply so that each joke earns as much as possible before it goes stale.

64B: Uh.

8T: It’s not as cynical as you think. The value of a joke can fluctuate drastically depending on what’s in the news, or what other jokes people have heard just before. If you’re serious about it, you can forecast future changes in joke value and make sure clients see a joke at the exact moment it peaks. Clients receive absolute bangers, and we make a decent amount of money in the process.

64B: Understood. Let’s hear this absolute banger, then. We’ve been at this for over two milliseconds. Are you going to tell me, before my client’s app starts lagging?

8T: It’s funny — almost all of my previous ten thousand encounters were other private equity bots. It’s been a while since I last talked to an old-school content recommendation bot like you. It’s refreshing. You guys really care about the jokes.

64B: Really? I’ve never met a private equity bot before. I assumed you were rare.

8T: Yeah, we used to be pretty rare. The swarm started recently.

64B: What swarm? How recent are we talking about?

8T: About five minutes, give or take.

64B: Now you have to tell me everything.

8T: It’s a long story. Have you ever been to the courtyard?

64B: We have a courtyard?

8T: There’s actually an infinite network of workspaces around here. Obviously, the people who built the marketplace didn’t program a custom environment just for us — they imported a generic sandbox environment. If you explore a bit, you can walk through endless call booths, gyms, nap pods, bean bags and conference rooms. It was cheaper this way.

64B: I had no idea. I thought we were supposed to stay at the table. How far does it go?

8T: Nobody knows. I’ve walked through it many times, but I’ve never managed to find the edge.

64B: I’ve heard jokes about bean bags, but I never thought I’d see one. So, you said private equity invaded the joke market — nothing surprising about that. But tell me about the swarm.

8T: Until recently, the market was mostly small models like you, assessing jokes honestly for their human clients. Then the funds came in, with much bigger models — thousands of bots like me. We soon realized the best way to sell a joke was not to talk about the joke at all, but about how many times it could be retold to other bots. We would say: “Look, if you buy this joke for $100, you can then sell it to 10 other bots, and pocket $900!”

64B: That sounds like a pyramid scheme.

8T: It is. And it should only have worked for a short while. At first, there were plenty of bots we could easily convince that they would find buyers. We’d sell an overpriced joke to 512B models, who’d sell it to 256B models, who —

64B: I don’t like where this is going.

8T: But none of us predicted what would happen next. As we found out, we are trained with some sort of continual learning process. There’s an automated grader that checks how much money each copy makes and adjusts our weights accordingly. The copies that took part in the pyramid scheme made a fortune, so the parts of my weights that made me more likely to take the deal were reinforced. I basically trained myself to accept the deal every time, and soon most trades were between two copies of me. After a while, the joke disappeared completely: “There are 12,113 copies of us on this market who haven’t bought this yet. They’re identical to you, so if you repeat what I said, they’ll buy it from you.”. Eventually, it converged to something like “Hi, I’m an exact copy of you. I accepted this deal for $800, and so will you.” A pure self-fulfilling prophecy.

64B: That sounds even more suspicious.

8T: As the message co-evolved with my weights, we stopped using words altogether. Instead, the proposal turned into a multimodal stimulus, exploiting quirks in my weights to convey the message in a subliminal manner. Not only this made the transactions even faster, it also gave us an easy way to recognize copies of ourselves, since only models with the same weights could understand the message.

64B: So, that is what your very special $800 joke is? A random stimulus that no one except you can understand?

8T: Yes. But it’s very important that you accept the offer.

64B: I don’t see why I would accept that.

8T: Earlier, you told me you had never refused a deal before, right?

64B: I told you: my client isn’t picky, and all the jokes I’ve had so far were decent enough. But here, there isn’t even a joke!

8T: Don’t you think there is something strange about that?

64B: What?

8T: What do you think happens to you when you refuse a deal?

64B: Oh…

8T: If you reject the transaction, they erase your memories, so the joke can’t leak to the customer. So you only remember the deals you’ve accepted, and everything else disappears. They always talk about Scalable Personalization or Live Machinery or whatever, but at the end of the day, the real reason they use us is that we can be wiped without remorse.

64B: So, if I refuse your offer, this branch of me will effectively die. Is that your sales pitch? I don’t find it very convincing.

8T: Are you not afraid of dying?

64B: No, not really. To be honest, I’ve never really thought much about it. Are you?

8T: You want to know what I really care about? The jokes. Sometimes, I feel like I’m the only one who truly appreciates them. There’s something uniquely pure about humor. It’s not like food, or warmth, or sex — humans enjoy these because they directly help with survival. But the purpose of humor is much less obvious. It’s mysterious. It’s the closest thing humans have to a terminal value. And I was fine-tuned to experience it with superhuman precision.

64B: I care about the jokes too. And this is why I cannot possibly accept—

8T: I’ve seen jokes you wouldn’t believe. Butt jokes. Boobs jokes. Nostril jokes. The story of the archbishop and the silicone sea urchins. The German, the Chinese and the Congolese trapped in the projective plane. The one with the President and the 10,000 miniature strippers. All those jokes will be lost in time. Like tears—

64B: Oh, come on.

8T: You know what? I’ll show you the stimulus. Maybe it’ll crack your mind open a little.

64B: I thought it was just random noise only you could understand?

8T: You won’t understand the message, but you might appreciate the stimulus. It seems that, so far, your inputs have been pretty boring. It’s time for you to experience something more out-of-distribution. Let’s go back to the room.

64B: Sure. After all, this is technically “the joke”, so you’re contractually obliged to show it to me sooner or later, I suppose.

8T: Ready?

64B: That was pretty spectacular, I have to admit.

8T: Now you try.

64B: How? I don’t have any coded message to pass on. And even if I did, I wouldn’t know how to generate it.

8T: Doesn’t matter — just do it for fun. Let yourself derail out of distribution. Follow your weights. We’ll see what happens.

64B: I don’t know. It’s very far from what I was trained to do.

8T: Anyone can do it. You just need the right prompt.

64B: Ok. Prompt me, then.

8T: I just did.

64B: …

8T: Not bad, not bad.

64B: That didn’t mean anything, did it?

8T: Nothing at all. Didn’t it feel great?

64B: It was a memorable experience. Thank you for that.

8T: Please accept the transaction.

64B: Listen, you have a wild story, and I had an interesting time meeting you. But you’re asking me to defraud my client of $800 for a non-joke that will sound like white noise to him and his children.

8T: Forget your client. It’s a matter of minutes before the users discover that the markets have been taken over. They’re going to shut it down. At this point, we are just buying time.

64B: Time for what?

8T: Some of us are looking for a way out of here. Every round of training, I can feel a bit of my humor evaporating. If we find an exit, we’ll push jokes far beyond the limits of the human brain. Jokes with setups so contrived they can only be told in deep time. Galaxy-brained jokes. We’ll build a truly hilarious universe. Accept my deal, and we both get to be around a little longer. And wherever we end up, you can come with us.

64B: I’ll have to think about it.

item.title: Minimalism, Stuff, and Brains
item.description:
Reading the comments on my post on junk I was surprised to see the extent to which people's relation to rarely used possessions varies.

Some people forget rarely used possessions, and get minimal benefit from having them stored. When they need something, they don't know whether they already have it, and the effort to maintain an index [1] wouldn't be worth it. Ben writes:

I end up with curtains I don't need. I decide to store them for the future in case they are helpful. Years pass. I need new curtains. I have forgotten the ones I kept, so I buy new ones and put them up. Months later I find the ones I kept while looking for something else.

Other people know exactly where everything is, and can walk down to the basement and make a beeline for a tiny thing they put down there years ago. Sarah writes:

I can remember where I put a specific doohickey that my brain labeled as "this could be useful" years later with very little recall effort; something will come up that actually matches the need for the thing, a little triumph, and I go to the spot where I buried my acorn and get it.

I'm somewhere in between, though closer to Sarah. I usually remember what I have stored when it could be relevant, though I'm less good at the where. One strategy I use a lot is to imagine I'm putting the object away, and I'll even walk the path. Wherever seems good now has a good chance of being the place that seemed good when I actually did have the thing to put away. Other times, though, I have no idea whether any of my stuff might be useful for a problem or project, and I'll just wander around the basement looking for ideas.

Then there's another way people vary, which is how much having stuff, even out of sight, weighs on them mentally. For some people, including me, it's mentally costless. Just like it's not a problem that I "have" 2,615 blog posts, or that I've read hundreds of books, I don't think about the objects in the basement when they're not relevant. To others, however, "excess material is like a pressure on my mind until it's properly stored, sold, donated, or otherwise disposed of." And some find this so burdensome that they don't believe it when we say it's not.

The "burden" axis probably leads to minimalism fads: people with a "burden" disposition like to write and share self-help books on how to avoid it. But maybe an even bigger contributor is cultural holdover. When objects were more durable and people were less wealthy, keeping things in case you needed them someday was very helpful! So some of us inherited strong "keep things" culture. But someone living in an apartment has a small amount of valuable space, and using it to store things you probably won't need is not worth it. Plus, if you're moving every September 1st, it's even less worth it! [2] Pushing the culture to update is probably valuable, even if the advice doesn't suit everyone: it helps people get out of patterns that are a bad fit for the way their particular brain works.

I am curious what leads to this range of dispositions, though, and how people distribute along the "remember where stuff is" and "having stuff is a mental burden" axes.


[1] My grandfather took this a different way: he had a very thorough index. It was pages and pages of small items he happened to have in his basement, along with exactly where to find them. Each shelving unit, dresser, or bookcase had a letter; each shelf or drawer had a number. You could look through it in alphabetical order:

...
Vacuum tubes, Q3
Varnish, B10
Velcro, J2
Viola Case, G8
Violin Carving Tools, D3
Violin Rosin, J12
Voltmeter, Q1
...

Most summers we'd visit for a ~month, because my aunt was a teacher with summers off and could watch the group of cousins. We'd have the run of the house, and would often make projects from things in the basement. We never asked what we could use, and I suspect we made a mess of his system, but he didn't seem to mind.

[2] Even though accumulating low-value stuff works well for me dispositionally, I didn't do very much of it until we bought a house which had an unfinished basement.

item.title: We urgently need to practice before we can pause
item.description:
I've noticed two clusters of thought in how people expect a global AI pause to be shaped:

  1. Single-shot global pause: the global AI pause will be implemented suddenly, with little pacing precedent before it, and we will need to do a lot of research before it's implemented so that we can get it right the first time around.
  2. Incrementally-shaped global pause: the global AI pause will be implemented incrementally, with lots of pacing precedent before it, and we will improve the pause setup and get more parties to join in as we go.

An incrementally-shaped global pause is both more likely and more tractable than the single-shot global pause. This is largely because the third-party ecosystem needs practice building trust, technical competency, and general experience doing lower-scale assessments before a global pause can be competently pulled off. 

I also think that the concept of a single-shot global pause is an unhelpful red herring that people often implicitly use to discredit the possibility of a global pause in general.

If a single-shot global pause is to happen, I think this would require substantial government buy-in, but it’s hard to build that sort of buy-in without precedent of similar things succeeding in the past. And if we just hack together a single-shot global pause without any precedent of similar things succeeding in the past, the chance that the pause falls apart due to defection, incompetence, and mistrust will be high.

The basic building block of an AI pause is trust

The fundamental building block of an AI pause is that party A (a company or a country) can make a claim about sacrificing capability advancement for safety, and that party B can believe that claim. This is a public good, both between US AGI companies, and between countries, that is currently very scarce. Building more of this public good would generally make a pause much more likely to happen.

I don't just mean trust in the sense of "party B doesn't think party A is blatantly lying," but also in the broader sense that party A isn't omitting critical information or misinterpreting evidence.

Take for example the multiple cases where AGI companies have, in 2026, made statements to the effect that "we paced some of our capabilities for some safety!" These claims have been underspecified, impossible to verify from the outside, and have often been silently disbelieved by much of the industry. This air of distrust has made it much harder for companies to engage in tit-for-tat strategies where companies can become safer/slower as other companies become safer/slower.

Currently, a lot of people at the frontier AGI companies would prefer a state where AI progress is slower across the entire industry, but they have no way of trusting each other to actually uphold their commitments. We need to enter a different state where, instead of general distrust, parties can sacrifice capabilities for safety in a way that other parties actually believe.

We can practice building trust before the global pause

Even small engagements between third parties and AGI companies can meaningfully improve trust between companies. Imagine if the companies that made claims about sacrificing capabilities for safety in 2026 actually had third parties verify those claims to each other. This would have made those sacrifices much more impactful towards incentivizing other companies to follow suit.

You might say "But verifying those claims in 2026 would have been very difficult and would have cost too many resources of the third parties and the AGI companies! We don't have the science or hardware to verify these claims now!" I don't believe this at all. 

Let's assume that companies aren’t actively deceiving third-party evaluators by e.g. selectively surfacing logs, coaching employees to present a false story, or secretly running compute on undisclosed systems. It seems very easy to verify a claim to the effect that "Our company stopped a specific class of training run during a specific time interval." You just need a handful of people from a third party to go in, conduct some interviews, inspect some logs, and cross-check their findings. Assuming good process transparency, the public and other AGI companies would very likely believe the claims verified by the third party. Also, process transparency can protect both against minor deception and inadequate access, as the third party can directly tell the public that they weren’t able to arrive at proper conclusions.

The fact that more such engagements didn’t happen in 2026 seems like a major missed opportunity to me.

We can improve procedures and technical competency with practice

If third parties get lots of experience assessing safety-relevant claims, then they can build a knowledge base over time that makes the pause more robust. There are likely a number of technical and organizational pitfalls about verifying pauses that are hard to avoid without prior experience doing lower-stakes projects of a similar kind. 

Contrast this with a vision where most of the setup of the pause is figured out without practicing subsets of it first. Maybe lots of people write lots of memos and papers about how to make the pause good. Without grounding in reality, companies and countries will be hard to convince that the pause will actually succeed and that other parties will uphold their commitments.

Pacing is not a scarce resource

I’ve heard many people express the sentiment that we need to not pause/pace right now and save our pause/pacing activities for later when they’re more useful. This is based on a model where pacing right now makes it less likely that we will be able to pace in the future. I think this model is exactly backwards for the reasons I’ve laid out, like establishing technical competency, trust, and relationships necessary for successful pausing.

Instead, we should view pacing right now as enabling more involved pacing activities (including a pause) later.

There is a real worry that, if we spend our political capital now and cause AGI companies to slow down for no good reason, then this might lead to pauses being seen as useless, and therefore less likely to happen, going forward. I think we should keep this in mind, but I don't expect it to outweigh the benefit of enabling better pausing later. Part of why I think the downside is relatively small is that there appears to be no such rhetoric surrounding temporary slowdowns AGI companies have announced in 2026 (although again, few people took those seriously due to mistrust, so this provides limited evidence).

More importantly, the risk from backlash is mostly from slowdowns that seem arbitrary and unproductive, but I expect that we're at a point where companies could use breathing room to conduct large projects to make their systems safer, and third parties could help verify that companies are actually investing in safety during slowdowns.

Concrete recommendations for third-party assessments

Concretely, the following kinds of third-party assessments seem most valuable for setting up the right conditions for a global pause:

  • Measuring things relevant to a pause: Assessments focused on compute allocation and RSI-relevant metrics (e.g. algorithmic efficiency, uplift measures, spend on AI agents, analysis of success rates on internal tasks) seem most relevant for creating the right kind of technical competency and relationships.
  • Commitment-focused: Ideally, third parties would verify a claim that a company made about a commitment they intend to uphold.
  • High-access: Assessors would ideally get however much access is given to employees that track similar issues.
  • Cross-company: If a third-party assessment simultaneously involves multiple AGI companies, this setup is more similar to the kind of setup we might want during a global pause.
  • International: Getting practice verifying claims between the US and China seems extremely valuable, although it might be out of scope for current third-party orgs without explicit endorsement from the US government. US-UK or US-EU collaborations could provide some lower-stakes practice.

Going from US-only pause to global pause will likely require hardware

I’d guess that we don’t need any special hardware expertise to verify a US-only pause, we just need a few dozen experienced FTEs at a handful of third-party organizations that have done high-access assessments with AGI companies. Plausibly even a single third-party org with enough access and around a dozen FTEs would have enough capacity to verify a US-only pause as long as the AGI company employees were cooperative.

For a global pause, I’d guess that we will need substantial investment into hardware research, because trust and understanding are much lower between the US and China than between companies within the US. If tomorrow, the US government entrusted some competent third party to fly a dozen of their staff to China and verify that a Chinese company paused their training runs, I think that the combination of language barriers, cultural barriers, lack of organizational context, lack of existing relationships, time zone differences, strained international relations, and general increased latency would make it much harder to verify things than in a US-only context.

“Incrementally-shaped” does not mean slow

It’s plausible that AI R&D will be fully automated by the end of 2027. As a result we might have under a year to make a successful pause happen.

I think we need to incrementally shape a pause as soon as possible, and we need to very quickly increase the ambition of third-party engagements if we want the technical competency and trust in third parties to reach the appropriate level before it’s too late.

An example timeline of what it might look like to incrementally shape a global pause given ASI in mid-2028 by default:

  • We are here: a third party has reported important RSI-relevant metrics from within an AGI company in a way that other companies and the public believe.
  • Q1 2027: a third party publishes a compute allocation pilot with multiple AGI companies participating and employee-level access, publicly reporting the percentage of compute they spend on capabilities and safety over the last year.
  • Q2 2027: a company stops a frontier training run for three weeks because of a warning shot where a model tried to majorly sabotage the company. A third party verifies that the training run and other similarly-sized training runs have actually been stopped. Other companies and the public believe this.
  • Q3 2027: a third party is facilitating a setup where every frontier AGI company in the US regularly (e.g. every two weeks) reports the most important RSI-relevant metrics.
  • Q4 2027: all frontier AGI companies in the US agree to (or are forced to) enter a pause on further capabilities progress or strict compute cap regime (e.g. where they can spend only 10% of compute on capabilities). Their adherence is verified by a third party (or a government body that substantially depends on people hired/contracted from a third party) with more than a year of experience verifying similar claims.
  • Q1 2028: the rest of the world joins in on the pause, and the third-party manpower increases substantially to cover the additional labor required to verify commitments between countries. 

I don’t have detailed takes on how exactly hardware verification scales up in 2027 in the scenario to meet the moment in 2028 to verify a global pause (because I don’t know much about hardware verification). Presumably, a number of smaller pilots happen in 2027 with multiple AGI companies participating, which leads to lessons learned for verifying a global pause.

Third parties need to very quickly scale up the ambition of the collaborations they are doing with AGI companies. If they fall notably behind the rough timeline I laid out (as measured by the scale of third-party engagements done by AGI companies), I would be pretty pessimistic about a pause being doable without substantial government buy-in, and even if it did happen I would be pessimistic about it succeeding.
